# Practical considerations

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Common fitting problems

### Convergence failure

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
Usually one of four things:

- [Poor starting values]{style="color: tomato;"}: the search moves into parameter values where the model or the solver breaks down
- A [flat likelihood surface]{style="color: tomato;"} in some direction, so there is no gradient to follow
- [Poorly scaled parameters]{style="color: tomato;"}, as [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} and [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"} were today; a [log transformation]{style="color: tomato;"} fixed it
- [Numerical instability]{style="color: tomato;"} at parameter bounds, or missing bounds where they were needed
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Parameter identifiability problems

- [Multiple solutions]{style="color: tomato;"}: several parameter combinations fit equally well, so the estimate depends on the starting value
- [Correlated parameters]{style="color: tomato;"}: only a combination such as the ratio [$\beta / \gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is determined by the data
- [Insufficient data]{style="color: tomato;"} or an [overparameterised model]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Remedies for identifiability problems

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- [Multiple starting values]{style="color: tomato;"}, checking that they converge to the same estimate
- [Profile likelihoods or posterior distributions]{style="color: tomato;"} for each parameter, not point estimates alone
- [Fixing parameters]{style="color: tomato;"} known from other sources, or placing [informative priors]{style="color: tomato;"} on them
- [Additional data]{style="color: tomato;"} that inform the parameters the outbreak curve cannot
- [Model reduction]{style="color: tomato;"}: simplify until the model is identifiable, then add complexity back one piece at a time
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Implausible estimates

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- Check the [model assumptions]{style="color: tomato;"} against what is known about the disease and the setting
- Check [data quality]{style="color: tomato;"}: reporting changes, backfilled counts, case definitions that changed during the outbreak
- [Residual analysis]{style="color: tomato;"}: a pattern in the residuals over time indicates a missing process in the model
- [Sensitivity analysis]{style="color: tomato;"}: how much the estimates move when uncertain assumptions are changed
- Fit [alternative models]{style="color: tomato;"} and compare them formally
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Best practices

### Before fitting

- Plot the data and understand how they were collected
- Check the model assumptions against the setting
- Set realistic [parameter bounds or priors]{style="color: tomato;"} before fitting
- Prepare several starting values

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### While fitting

- [Monitor convergence]{style="color: tomato;"} of the optimiser or the chain, rather than reading only the final estimate
- Check for [local optima]{style="color: tomato;"} by comparing runs from different starting values
- [Document every fit]{style="color: tomato;"}, including the ones that failed

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### After fitting

- Assess [goodness of fit]{style="color: tomato;"} by plotting the fitted model over the data with its uncertainty
- Report [confidence or credible intervals]{style="color: tomato;"}, not point estimates alone
- Carry out a [sensitivity analysis]{style="color: tomato;"} of the conclusions to the assumptions
- [Validate predictions]{style="color: tomato;"} on data not used in fitting

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Software

### R packages

-   [`bbmle`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bbmle/vignettes/mle.pdf): maximum likelihood, profiles and confidence intervals, as used today
-   [`rstan`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/rstan.pdf) and [`cmdstanr`](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/): Stan from R
-   [`pomp`](https://kingaa.github.io/pomp/vignettes/getting_started.html): particle filtering and particle MCMC
-   [`brms`](https://paul-buerkner.github.io/brms/index.html): Bayesian regression models with Stan underneath
-   [`nimble`](https://r-nimble.org/): Bayesian models with your own choice of MCMC algorithm

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Other software

-   [`Stan`](https://mc-stan.org): the probabilistic programming language behind `rstan`, `cmdstanr` and `brms`
-   [`OpenBUGS`](https://sourceforge.net/p/openbugs/wiki/Home/) and [`JAGS`](https://mcmc-jags.sourceforge.io): the older generation of Gibbs samplers, still widely used
-   [`PyMC`](https://www.pymc.io/welcome.html): Bayesian inference in Python
-   [`Turing.jl`](https://turinglang.org/): Bayesian inference in Julia
